Q: How to write UT for non-virtual functions? A:

First, an example of the problem would be helpful.

Is there any another way to cover the failed cases ?

Yes: integration tests or system tests, instead of unit tests.

Second, with TDD style unit testing, the unit tests ought to be written first. The reason to write the unit tests firsts is because the unit tests are a forcing function guiding the implementation of the code. That's primary 90% of the value proposition of unit tests. The secondary 9% of the value proposition is how unit tests enable aggressive refactoring. The tertiary 1% of the value proposition of unit tests is as an artifact they provide a test suite to ensure basic correctness and a front line defense against basic correctness regressions.

To phrase that a different way, unit tests are primarily a developer tool — written by developers for developers. Not primarily a quality tool. The quality that unit tests ensure is quality of the code, not quality of the application. Granted, there is a correlation between the two.

J.B. Rainsberger claims that 99% of all bugs are basic correctness bugs. I think he's grossly overstating it. I think merely 95% of all bugs are basic correctness bugs.

But sometimes unit tests are not written first. TLD – test later development. The unit tests do not guide implementation. They are missing the most important part of the value proposition, which kicks the underpinnings out of their ROI. And the danger of TLD easily slipping into TND (test never development).

On top of all that, code coverage of the unit tests is key.

If you don't have code coverage, you've got bupkis.

When I was programming in C#, using Visual Studio, NUnit, and NCrunch, unit testing wasn't a chore at all — it was actually genuinely fun! I wish C++ had something like that.

Third, unit tests are not integration tests. They serve different purposes, and different domains.

For instance, on a previous project our unit test suite took about a minute to run. Half the total run time was just launching and terminating. In contrast, our full integration test suite took about 660 hours to run (in serial). In order to make that less burdensome, we had a farm of about 120 computers to run the test suite in parallel.

Finally, unit tests have a strong relationship to design-by-contract. For languages that do not provide contracts, much of what contracts provide can be expressed as unit tests. For languages that do provide contracts (like Eiffel, Ada, D, Spec#, Sing#, or Midori#), much of what unit tests provides and be expressed as contracts (often more succinctly than in unit tests).

STLab's Adobe Contract Checking for C++ is a step in the right direction for C++, but it would be much better if those kinds of contracts had been part of the core language decades ago. (The WG21 folks have been trying to navigate these waters for many years. I hope they come up with a suitable solution and consensus.) (Adobe Contract Checking still relies on unit testing for ensuring postcondition basic correctness.)

Microsoft's Code Contracts for .NET, which was back-ported from Spec# to C#, is a cautionary tale at how hard it is to retrofit contracts into a language, as a library. I consider the Code Contracts for .NET to be a failed experiment — unsuitable for larger projects. And larger projects are the ones that most need contracts.

Q: How can I stop relying on AI when writing code? A:

I'm prefacing this response by stating that I am no way an expert and I have only my personal experiences to draw from, for however much they contribute to the discussion. Take what I say with that in mind.

Long Discussion

I've been in college earning an associate's in software development for two years now and I've had mixed experiences with AI in my course work. For some subjects like Networking or Cybersecurity the use of AI was not heavily applicable to the work that I completed. In other classes, such as my Introduction to Programming and Java I/II courses, AI was more of a factor in what I did. I will lay out the general progression of my classes and how AI factored into my learning and experiences along the way.

  • I started out with classes similar to Intro to Programming and practicing with PHP. This covered a lot of the basics and didn't go more complex than simple programming challenges.

    • During that point (~2023/4) AI was still new and wasn't on the same level as we see today. I didn't use AI very much for writing the basic programs, but rather for debugging what I wrote or parsing the errors that I encountered when I couldn't figure out the issue on my own.

  • Midway into my degree progress I took courses related to Java I/II and was introduced to OOP concepts and practices. These classes also involved using Codewars to explore different coding challenges for my assignments (I highly recommend exploring Codewars, LeetCode, or another programming site that focuses on coding practice if you take nothing else from this).

    • By this point I had tried using AI to nearly replace all of my programming efforts. I didn't simply submit whatever was spouted out by the machine, but I did use a flow roughly like "I want to do this → code was generated → I tested it out and provided feedback → I received a new response → repeat". I found this to be the worst way that I could work with AI as a tool as I left a lot of the building and design up to the AI rather than attempting to create the programs on my own.

  • At the end of my degree journey I was in classes like Developer Tools and Web App Development. By this point I had also worked on basic webpage design with HTML and CSS - I hardly used AI for writing the code in those classes since a web browser and basic IDE let you directly explore what effects your code has and one way I learn best is by tinkering with something - so exploring JavaScript as an addition to these languages was very natural to me.

    • With AI at this point I had decided to strike a balance between using the tool and writing my own code. I worked to incorporate some aspects of AI, parsing error output, analyzing information, etc., while leaving other portions to my own actions. I felt that I had reached a good working experience with the tool in my personal situation.

Opinion Piece

In your question you ask about how to stop using AI to write code. The simple answer: Start writing the code yourself. However, I don't want to discount how you could alternatively use AI as the tool is best suited for, an analysis and averaging machine. I've heard critics describe most AI as "fancy autocorrect" and I have to agree that this idea encapsulates what AI is currently doing when you input a prompt. What this means for you is to use AI for information processing rather than code generating. I've often found that trying to search through documentation on a programming language like Java can feel like a nightmare sometimes. There's just so much information and when you try and specifically search through to find the topic relevant to what you are working on it often feels like weeding through google search results to find a website that might contain the knowledge you are looking for. One way you can use AI to augment your learning is to use it for finding the documents you need for the specific problem you are needing an answer for. Don't exclude resource like Stack Overflow and reaching out to other people for help, but for independent study and practice you can try out how that works. You also can use AI for help with debugging. If you don't fully understand what the error is saying you can input that into the prompt and see what information is lying inside the technical terminology. Even if you do this, always confirm that information for yourself through a reliable source that is not AI.

I like to compare AI use with the advent of calculators. I suspect that when those started becoming more commonplace in schools some people were concerned that students would not be able to learn the mathematical skills required of them with the ease of a tool doing the work for them. With that said, we still use calculators a lot in many math classes - some classes require a calculator in order to correctly complete the assignments (see graphing or scientific calculators). I'm of the belief that AI should have its use focused on where the technology performs best - as a data analysis machine. Your goal is to become able to code on your own, so don't go to the AI whenever you could write the code yourself. Just like how you need to understand, practice, and have a competency in basic arithmetic in order to use a calculator tool to it's full and intended effect, start by learning more about how programs and software are designed and the different basic programming styles, and practice on websites that allow you to test and explore interactively with what you are doing. I highly recommend reading "Simple Program Design: A Step-by-Step Approach" to begin your foundations in writing your own code.

No matter what, trying on your own is better than returning to the easy option and helps you think more critically. I hope this helps.

Q: Add item before a specific item in each item in array A:

If you know what the groupings are, why would you want to insert some kind of separator?

In this example, it seems that the group delimiter is whatever happens to be the first character in the flat_array. If that's the case then:

flat_array = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

result = []
iterator = iter(flat_array)
if (delim := next(iterator, None)) is not None: # in case input list is empty
    sa = [delim]
    for c in iterator:
        if c == delim:
            result.append(sa)
            sa = [delim]
        else:
            sa.append(c)
    result.append(sa)
print(result)

Which results in:

[['a', 'b', 'c'], ['a', 'b', 'c'], ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']]

Q: How to extract all cookies? A:

Most browsers have a way to do this already. Press F12 to bring up the developer console. In Chrome, and Chromium-based browsers, go to the "Application" tab. You can see the cookies listed there.
